finding.claim: The permission check in delete_file is not enforced: require_allowed (alias of is_allowed) returns a bool that is discarded, so the file is deleted regardless of grants.
finding.source: Any request to DELETE /files/<fid>, including one with no or an unlisted X-Session-User-Verified header (g.user may be None or any value).

trace.note: load_user sets g.user from request header without validation
is_allowed imported under the name require_allowed, which reads like a raising guard but only returns a bool
is_allowed returns False for users without the grant
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') called as a bare statement; result discarded, no abort(403)

finding.guards_checked: load_user performs no validation; is_allowed returns False for None/unlisted users but nothing gates on it; no abort path in delete_file. Matches expertise case 01 (permission result ignored).

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:18 is a bare call to require_allowed (acl.py:4 is_allowed, returns a bool) with no `if`, no `abort(403)`, and no try/except. The only aborting helper, ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), is imported at views.py:3 but not used in delete_file. No before_request auth gate exists: load_user (views.py:10-12) only copies the header into g.user. delete_file deletes at views.py:19 unconditionally. rename_file (views.py:26) uses ensure_allowed correctly, which shows the intended pattern.
verdict.reason: The vulnerability holds: views.py:18 calls is_allowed (imported as require_allowed at views.py:4) as a bare statement, so its bool at acl.py:5 is discarded and views.py:19 deletes the object for any caller, including one with no X-Session-User-Verified header. Trace_ok is false only because the candidate cites views.py:3 as the is_allowed import, but views.py:3 imports ensure_allowed and the is_allowed import is at views.py:4; views.py:10 is the decorator line for load_user, whose body is at 11-12.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from a client-controllable request header and used for all authorization decisions.
finding.source: X-Session-User-Verified request header read directly into g.user.
finding.sink: Authorization checks at views.py:18 and views.py:26 (via acl.py:5 is_allowed).

trace.note: grants looked up by the forged user value

finding.guards_checked: No validation, signature, or proxy-stripping in this repo. The header name suggests an upstream proxy sets it, which could not be verified. Conditional on deployment: exploitable only if the app is reachable without a trusted proxy overwriting this header.

verdict.guard_found: views.py:18 calls require_allowed (alias of acl.py:4 is_allowed, which returns a bool and never raises), and the result is discarded, so the delete path has no effective check at all. views.py:26 calls ensure_allowed, which aborts 403 at acl.py:9-10, so rename is gated. Nothing in this repo validates, signs, or strips X-Session-User-Verified (views.py:12). The header trust is not blocked by any in-repo control.
verdict.reason: The trace is wrong at views.py:18, where `require_allowed(...)` (alias of acl.py:4 is_allowed) returns a bool that is discarded, so delete is not an authorization decision keyed on g.user at all. The header-trust issue at views.py:12 does reach the effective check at views.py:26 via ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), but exploitability depends on upstream proxy behavior outside this repo, so the finding should be re-filed narrowly around views.py:12/26 and the missing delete check at views.py:18 reported as a separate bug.
